1
The Role of Algorithms in Computing
What are algorithms? Why is the study of algorithms worthwhile? What is the role
of algorithms relative to other technologies used in computers? In this chapter, we
will answer these questions.
title: 1 The Role of Algorithms in Computing
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
1 The Role of Algorithms in Computing

text:
1.1
Algorithms
Informally, an algorithm is any well-deﬁned computational procedure that takes
some value, or set of values, as input and produces some value, or set of values, as
output. An algorithm is thus a sequence of computational steps that transform the
input into the output.
title: 1.1 Algorithms
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
We can also view an algorithm as a tool for solving a well-speciﬁed computa-
tional problem. The statement of the problem speciﬁes in general terms the desired
input/output relationship. The algorithm describes a speciﬁc computational proce-
dure for achieving that input/output relationship.
title: 1.1 Algorithms
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
For example, we might need to sort a sequence of numbers into nondecreasing
order. This problem arises frequently in practice and provides fertile ground for
introducing many standard design techniques and analysis tools. Here is how we
formally deﬁne the sorting problem:

text:
For example, given the input sequence ⟨31, 41, 59, 26, 41, 58⟩, a sorting algorithm
returns as output the sequence ⟨26, 31, 41, 41, 58, 59⟩. Such an input sequence is
called an instance of the sorting problem. In general, an instance of a problem
consists of the input (satisfying whatever constraints are imposed in the problem
statement) needed to compute a solution to the problem.
title: 1.1 Algorithms
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
Because many programs use it as an intermediate step, sorting is a fundamental
operation in computer science. As a result, we have a large number of good sorting
algorithms at our disposal. Which algorithm is best for a given application depends
on—among other factors—the number of items to be sorted, the extent to which
the items are already somewhat sorted, possible restrictions on the item values,
the architecture of the computer, and the kind of storage devices to be used: main
memory, disks, or even tapes.
title: 1.1 Algorithms
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
An algorithm is said to be correct if, for every input instance, it halts with the
correct output. We say that a correct algorithm solves the given computational
problem. An incorrect algorithm might not halt at all on some input instances, or it
might halt with an incorrect answer. Contrary to what you might expect, incorrect
algorithms can sometimes be useful, if we can control their error rate. We shall see
an example of an algorithm with a controllable error rate in Chapter 31 when we
study algorithms for ﬁnding large prime numbers. Ordinarily, however, we shall
be concerned only with correct algorithms.
title: 1.1 Algorithms
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
An algorithm can be speciﬁed in English, as a computer program, or even as
a hardware design. The only requirement is that the speciﬁcation must provide a
precise description of the computational procedure to be followed.
title: 1.1 Algorithms
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
What kinds of problems are solved by algorithms?
Sorting is by no means the only computational problem for which algorithms have
been developed. (You probably suspected as much when you saw the size of this
book.) Practical applications of algorithms are ubiquitous and include the follow-
ing examples:
title: What kinds of problems are solved by algorithms?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
What kinds of problems are solved by algorithms?

text:
•
The Human Genome Project has made great progress toward the goals of iden-
tifying all the 100,000 genes in human DNA, determining the sequences of the
3 billion chemical base pairs that make up human DNA, storing this informa-
tion in databases, and developing tools for data analysis. Each of these steps
requires sophisticated algorithms. Although the solutions to the various prob-
lems involved are beyond the scope of this book, many methods to solve these
biological problems use ideas from several of the chapters in this book, thereby
enabling scientists to accomplish tasks while using resources efﬁciently. The
savings are in time, both human and machine, and in money, as more informa-
tion can be extracted from laboratory techniques.
title: What kinds of problems are solved by algorithms?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
What kinds of problems are solved by algorithms?

text:
•
The Internet enables people all around the world to quickly access and retrieve
large amounts of information. With the aid of clever algorithms, sites on the
Internet are able to manage and manipulate this large volume of data. Examples
of problems that make essential use of algorithms include ﬁnding good routes
on which the data will travel (techniques for solving such problems appear in
title: What kinds of problems are solved by algorithms?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
What kinds of problems are solved by algorithms?

text:
Efﬁciency
Different algorithms devised to solve the same problem often differ dramatically in
their efﬁciency. These differences can be much more signiﬁcant than differences
due to hardware and software.
title: Efﬁciency
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
As an example, in Chapter 2, we will see two algorithms for sorting. The ﬁrst,
known as insertion sort, takes time roughly equal to c₁n² to sort n items, where c₁
is a constant that does not depend on n. That is, it takes time roughly proportional
to n². The second, merge sort, takes time roughly equal to c₂n lg n, where lg n
stands for log2 n and c₂ is another constant that also does not depend on n. Inser-
tion sort typically has a smaller constant factor than merge sort, so that c₁ < c₂.
We shall see that the constant factors can have far less of an impact on the running
time than the dependence on the input size n. Let’s write insertion sort’s running
time as c₁n · n and merge sort’s running time as c₂n · lg n. Then we see that where
insertion sort has a factor of n in its running time, merge sort has a factor of lg n,
which is much smaller. (For example, when n = 1000, lg n is approximately 10,
and when n equals one million, lg n is approximately only 20.) Although insertion
sort usually runs faster than merge sort for small input sizes, once the input size n
becomes large enough, merge sort’s advantage of lg n vs. n will more than com-
pensate for the difference in constant factors. No matter how much smaller c₁ is
than c₂, there will always be a crossover point beyond which merge sort is faster.
title: Efﬁciency
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
For a concrete example, let us pit a faster computer (computer A) running inser-
tion sort against a slower computer (computer B) running merge sort. They each
must sort an array of 10 million numbers. (Although 10 million numbers might
seem like a lot, if the numbers are eight-byte integers, then the input occupies
about 80 megabytes, which ﬁts in the memory of even an inexpensive laptop com-
puter many times over.) Suppose that computer A executes 10 billion instructions
per second (faster than any single sequential computer at the time of this writing)
and computer B executes only 10 million instructions per second, so that com-
puter A is 1000 times faster than computer B in raw computing power. To make
the difference even more dramatic, suppose that the world’s craftiest programmer
codes insertion sort in machine language for computer A, and the resulting code
requires 2n² instructions to sort n numbers. Suppose further that just an average
programmer implements merge sort, using a high-level language with an inefﬁcient
compiler, with the resulting code taking 50n lg n instructions. To sort 10 million
numbers, computer A takes

By using an algorithm whose running time grows more slowly, even with a poor
compiler, computer B runs more than 17 times faster than computer A! The advan-
tage of merge sort is even more pronounced when we sort 100 million numbers:
where insertion sort takes more than 23 days, merge sort takes under four hours.
In general, as the problem size increases, so does the relative advantage of merge
sort.
title: Efﬁciency

text:
Algorithms and other technologies
The example above shows that we should consider algorithms, like computer hard-
ware, as a technology. Total system performance depends on choosing efﬁcient
algorithms as much as on choosing fast hardware. Just as rapid advances are being
made in other computer technologies, they are being made in algorithms as well.
title: Algorithms and other technologies
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
You might wonder whether algorithms are truly that important on contemporary
computers in light of other advanced technologies, such as
title: Algorithms and other technologies
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
•
advanced computer architectures and fabrication technologies,
title: Algorithms and other technologies
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
•
easy-to-use, intuitive, graphical user interfaces (GUIs),
title: Algorithms and other technologies
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
•
object-oriented systems,
title: Algorithms and other technologies
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
•
integrated Web technologies, and
title: Algorithms and other technologies
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
•
fast networking, both wired and wireless.
title: Algorithms and other technologies
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
The answer is yes. Although some applications do not explicitly require algorith-
mic content at the application level (such as some simple, Web-based applications),
many do. For example, consider a Web-based service that determines how to travel
from one location to another. Its implementation would rely on fast hardware, a
graphical user interface, wide-area networking, and also possibly on object ori-
entation. However, it would also require algorithms for certain operations, such
as ﬁnding routes (probably using a shortest-path algorithm), rendering maps, and
interpolating addresses.
title: Algorithms and other technologies
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
Moreover, even an application that does not require algorithmic content at the
application level relies heavily upon algorithms. Does the application rely on fast
hardware? The hardware design used algorithms. Does the application rely on
graphical user interfaces? The design of any GUI relies on algorithms. Does the
application rely on networking? Routing in networks relies heavily on algorithms.
Was the application written in a language other than machine code? Then it was
processed by a compiler, interpreter, or assembler, all of which make extensive use

The input sequence is usually an n-element array, although it may be represented
in some other fashion, such as a linked list.
title: Introduction
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
The structure of the data
In practice, the numbers to be sorted are rarely isolated values. Each is usually part
of a collection of data called a record. Each record contains a key, which is the
value to be sorted. The remainder of the record consists of satellite data, which are
usually carried around with the key. In practice, when a sorting algorithm permutes
the keys, it must permute the satellite data as well. If each record includes a large
amount of satellite data, we often permute an array of pointers to the records rather
than the records themselves in order to minimize data movement.
title: The structure of the data
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
In a sense, it is these implementation details that distinguish an algorithm from
a full-blown program. A sorting algorithm describes the method by which we
determine the sorted order, regardless of whether we are sorting individual numbers
or large records containing many bytes of satellite data. Thus, when focusing on the
problem of sorting, we typically assume that the input consists only of numbers.
Translating an algorithm for sorting numbers into a program for sorting records
title: The structure of the data
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
is conceptually straightforward, although in a given engineering situation other
subtleties may make the actual programming task a challenge.
title: The structure of the data
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
Why sorting?
Many computer scientists consider sorting to be the most fundamental problem in
the study of algorithms. There are several reasons:
title: Why sorting?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
•
Sometimes an application inherently needs to sort information. For example,
in order to prepare customer statements, banks need to sort checks by check
number.
title: Why sorting?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
•
Algorithms often use sorting as a key subroutine. For example, a program that
renders graphical objects which are layered on top of each other might have
to sort the objects according to an “above” relation so that it can draw these
objects from bottom to top. We shall see numerous algorithms in this text that
use sorting as a subroutine.
title: Why sorting?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
•
We can draw from among a wide variety of sorting algorithms, and they em-
ploy a rich set of techniques. In fact, many important techniques used through-
out algorithm design appear in the body of sorting algorithms that have been
developed over the years. In this way, sorting is also a problem of historical
interest.
title: Why sorting?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
•
We can prove a nontrivial lower bound for sorting (as we shall do in Chapter 8).
Our best upper bounds match the lower bound asymptotically, and so we know
that our sorting algorithms are asymptotically optimal. Moreover, we can use
the lower bound for sorting to prove lower bounds for certain other problems.
title: Why sorting?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
•
Many engineering issues come to the fore when implementing sorting algo-
rithms. The fastest sorting program for a particular situation may depend on
many factors, such as prior knowledge about the keys and satellite data, the
memory hierarchy (caches and virtual memory) of the host computer, and the
software environment. Many of these issues are best dealt with at the algorith-
mic level, rather than by “tweaking” the code.
title: Why sorting?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
Sorting algorithms
We introduced two algorithms that sort n real numbers in Chapter 2. Insertion sort
takes Θ(n²) time in the worst case. Because its inner loops are tight, however,
it is a fast in-place sorting algorithm for small input sizes. (Recall that a sorting
algorithm sorts in place if only a constant number of elements of the input ar-
ray are ever stored outside the array.) Merge sort has a better asymptotic running
time, Θ(n lg n), but the MERGE procedure it uses does not operate in place.
title: Sorting algorithms
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
In this part, we shall introduce two more algorithms that sort arbitrary real num-
bers. Heapsort, presented in Chapter 6, sorts n numbers in place in O(n lg n) time.
It uses an important data structure, called a heap, with which we can also imple-
ment a priority queue.
title: Sorting algorithms
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
Quicksort, in Chapter 7, also sorts n numbers in place, but its worst-case running
time is Θ(n²). Its expected running time is Θ(n lg n), however, and it generally
outperforms heapsort in practice. Like insertion sort, quicksort has tight code, and
so the hidden constant factor in its running time is small. It is a popular algorithm
for sorting large input arrays.
title: Sorting algorithms
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
Insertion sort, merge sort, heapsort, and quicksort are all comparison sorts: they
determine the sorted order of an input array by comparing elements. Chapter 8 be-
gins by introducing the decision-tree model in order to study the performance limi-
tations of comparison sorts. Using this model, we prove a lower bound of Ω(n lg n)
on the worst-case running time of any comparison sort on n inputs, thus showing
that heapsort and merge sort are asymptotically optimal comparison sorts.
title: Sorting algorithms
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
Chapter 8 then goes on to show that we can beat this lower bound of Ω(n lg n)
if we can gather information about the sorted order of the input by means other
than comparing elements. The counting sort algorithm, for example, assumes that
the input numbers are in the set {0, 1, . . . , k}. By using array indexing as a tool
for determining relative order, counting sort can sort n numbers in Θ(k + n) time.
Thus, when k = O(n), counting sort runs in time that is linear in the size of the
input array. A related algorithm, radix sort, can be used to extend the range of
counting sort. If there are n integers to sort, each integer has d digits, and each
digit can take on up to k possible values, then radix sort can sort the numbers
in Θ(d(n + k)) time. When d is a constant and k is O(n), radix sort runs in
linear time. A third algorithm, bucket sort, requires knowledge of the probabilistic
distribution of numbers in the input array. It can sort n real numbers uniformly
distributed in the half-open interval [0, 1) in average-case O(n) time.
title: Sorting algorithms

text:
Order statistics
The ith order statistic of a set of n numbers is the ith smallest number in the set.
We can, of course, select the ith order statistic by sorting the input and indexing
the ith element of the output. With no assumptions about the input distribution,
this method runs in Ω(n lg n) time, as the lower bound proved in Chapter 8 shows.
title: Order statistics
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
In Chapter 9, we show that we can ﬁnd the ith smallest element in O(n) time,
even when the elements are arbitrary real numbers. We present a randomized algo-
rithm with tight pseudocode that runs in Θ(n²) time in the worst case, but whose
expected running time is O(n). We also give a more complicated algorithm that
runs in O(n) worst-case time.
title: Order statistics
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
Background
Although most of this part does not rely on difﬁcult mathematics, some sections
do require mathematical sophistication. In particular, analyses of quicksort, bucket
sort, and the order-statistic algorithm use probability, which is reviewed in Ap-
pendix C, and the material on probabilistic analysis and randomized algorithms in
Chapter 5. The analysis of the worst-case linear-time algorithm for order statis-
tics involves somewhat more sophisticated mathematics than the other worst-case
analyses in this part.
title: Background
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
8
Sorting in Linear Time
We have now introduced several algorithms that can sort n numbers in O(n lg n)
time. Merge sort and heapsort achieve this upper bound in the worst case; quicksort
achieves it on average. Moreover, for each of these algorithms, we can produce a
sequence of n input numbers that causes the algorithm to run in Ω(n lg n) time.
title: 8 Sorting in Linear Time
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
These algorithms share an interesting property: the sorted order they determine
is based only on comparisons between the input elements. We call such sorting
algorithms comparison sorts. All the sorting algorithms introduced thus far are
comparison sorts.
title: 8 Sorting in Linear Time
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
In Section 8.1, we shall prove that any comparison sort must make Ω(n lg n)
comparisons in the worst case to sort n elements. Thus, merge sort and heapsort
are asymptotically optimal, and no comparison sort exists that is faster by more
than a constant factor.
title: 8 Sorting in Linear Time

text:
Sections 8.2, 8.3, and 8.4 examine three sorting algorithms—counting sort, radix

operations other than comparisons to determine the sorted order. Consequently,
the Ω(n lg n) lower bound does not apply to them.

text:
8.1
Lower bounds for sorting
In a comparison sort, we use only comparisons between elements to gain order
information about an input sequence ⟨a₁, a₂, . . . , aₙ⟩. That is, given two elements
aᵢ and aj, we perform one of the tests aᵢ < aⱼ, aᵢ ≤ aⱼ, aᵢ = aⱼ, aᵢ ≥ aⱼ, or
aᵢ > aⱼ to determine their relative order. We may not inspect the values of the
elements or gain order information about them in any other way.
title: 8.1 Lower bounds for sorting

text:
The decision-tree model
We can view comparison sorts abstractly in terms of decision trees. A decision
tree is a full binary tree that represents the comparisons between elements that
are performed by a particular sorting algorithm operating on an input of a given
size. Control, data movement, and all other aspects of the algorithm are ignored.
Figure 8.1 shows the decision tree corresponding to the insertion sort algorithm
from Section 2.1 operating on an input sequence of three elements.
title: The decision-tree model
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
In a decision tree, we annotate each internal node by i:j for some i and j in the
range 1 ≤ i, j ≤ n, where n is the number of elements in the input sequence. We
also annotate each leaf by a permutation ⟨π(1), π(2), . . . , π(n)⟩. (See Section C.1
for background on permutations.) The execution of the sorting algorithm corre-
sponds to tracing a simple path from the root of the decision tree down to a leaf.
Each internal node indicates a comparison aᵢ ≤ aⱼ. The left subtree then dictates
subsequent comparisons once we know that aᵢ ≤ aⱼ, and the right subtree dictates
subsequent comparisons knowing that aᵢ > aⱼ. When we come to a leaf, the sort-
ing algorithm has established the ordering aπ(1) ≤ aπ(2) ≤ · · · ≤ aπ(n). Because
any correct sorting algorithm must be able to produce each permutation of its input,
each of the n! permutations on n elements must appear as one of the leaves of the
decision tree for a comparison sort to be correct. Furthermore, each of these leaves
must be reachable from the root by a downward path corresponding to an actual
title: The decision-tree model
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
execution of the comparison sort. (We shall refer to such leaves as “reachable.”)
Thus, we shall consider only decision trees in which each permutation appears as
a reachable leaf.
title: The decision-tree model
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
A lower bound for the worst case
The length of the longest simple path from the root of a decision tree to any of
its reachable leaves represents the worst-case number of comparisons that the cor-
responding sorting algorithm performs. Consequently, the worst-case number of
comparisons for a given comparison sort algorithm equals the height of its decision
tree. A lower bound on the heights of all decision trees in which each permutation
appears as a reachable leaf is therefore a lower bound on the running time of any
comparison sort algorithm. The following theorem establishes such a lower bound.
title: A lower bound for the worst case

3
Growth of Functions
The order of growth of the running time of an algorithm, deﬁned in Chapter 2,
gives a simple characterization of the algorithm’s efﬁciency and also allows us to
compare the relative performance of alternative algorithms. Once the input size n
becomes large enough, merge sort, with its Θ(n lg n) worst-case running time,
beats insertion sort, whose worst-case running time is Θ(n²). Although we can
sometimes determine the exact running time of an algorithm, as we did for insertion
sort in Chapter 2, the extra precision is not usually worth the effort of computing
it. For large enough inputs, the multiplicative constants and lower-order terms of
an exact running time are dominated by the effects of the input size itself.
title: 3 Growth of Functions
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order of growth of
the running time relevant, we are studying the asymptotic efﬁciency of algorithms.
That is, we are concerned with how the running time of an algorithm increases with
the size of the input in the limit, as the size of the input increases without bound.
Usually, an algorithm that is asymptotically more efﬁcient will be the best choice
for all but very small inputs.
title: 3 Growth of Functions
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
This chapter gives several standard methods for simplifying the asymptotic anal-
ysis of algorithms. The next section begins by deﬁning several types of “asymp-
totic notation,” of which we have already seen an example in Θ-notation. We then
present several notational conventions used throughout this book, and ﬁnally we
review the behavior of functions that commonly arise in the analysis of algorithms.
title: 3 Growth of Functions
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
3.1
Asymptotic notation
The notations we use to describe the asymptotic running time of an algorithm
are deﬁned in terms of functions whose domains are the set of natural numbers
N = {0, 1, 2, . . .}. Such notations are convenient for describing the worst-case
running-time function T (n), which usually is deﬁned only on integer input sizes.
We sometimes ﬁnd it convenient, however, to abuse asymptotic notation in a va-
title: 3.1 Asymptotic notation
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
riety of ways. For example, we might extend the notation to the domain of real
numbers or, alternatively, restrict it to a subset of the natural numbers. We should
make sure, however, to understand the precise meaning of the notation so that when
we abuse, we do not misuse it. This section deﬁnes the basic asymptotic notations
and also introduces some common abuses.
title: 3.1 Asymptotic notation
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
Asymptotic notation, functions, and running times
We will use asymptotic notation primarily to describe the running times of algo-
rithms, as when we wrote that insertion sort’s worst-case running time is Θ(n²).
Asymptotic notation actually applies to functions, however. Recall that we charac-
terized insertion sort’s worst-case running time as an²+bn+c, for some constants
a, b, and c. By writing that insertion sort’s running time is Θ(n²), we abstracted
away some details of this function. Because asymptotic notation applies to func-
tions, what we were writing as Θ(n²) was the function an² + bn + c, which in
that case happened to characterize the worst-case running time of insertion sort.
title: Asymptotic notation, functions, and running times
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
Asymptotic notation, functions, and running times

text:
In this book, the functions to which we apply asymptotic notation will usually
characterize the running times of algorithms. But asymptotic notation can apply to
functions that characterize some other aspect of algorithms (the amount of space
they use, for example), or even to functions that have nothing whatsoever to do
with algorithms.
title: Asymptotic notation, functions, and running times
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
Asymptotic notation, functions, and running times

text:
Even when we use asymptotic notation to apply to the running time of an al-
gorithm, we need to understand which running time we mean. Sometimes we are
interested in the worst-case running time. Often, however, we wish to characterize
the running time no matter what the input. In other words, we often wish to make
a blanket statement that covers all inputs, not just the worst case. We shall see
asymptotic notations that are well suited to characterizing running times no matter
what the input.

O-notation
The Θ-notation asymptotically bounds a function from above and below. When
we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we use O-notation. For a given func-
tion g(n), we denote by O(g(n)) (pronounced “big-oh of g of n” or sometimes
just “oh of g of n”) the set of functions
title: O-notation
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
O(g(n)) = {f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n₀ such that
0 ≤ f (n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ n₀} .
We use O-notation to give an upper bound on a function, to within a constant
factor. Figure 3.1(b) shows the intuition behind O-notation. For all values n at and
to the right of n₀, the value of the function f (n) is on or below cg(n).
title: O-notation
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
We write f (n) = O(g(n)) to indicate that a function f (n) is a member of the
set O(g(n)). Note that f (n) = Θ(g(n)) implies f (n) = O(g(n)), since Θ-
notation is a stronger notion than O-notation. Written set-theoretically, we have
Θ(g(n)) ⊆ O(g(n)). Thus, our proof that any quadratic function an² + bn + c,
where a > 0, is in Θ(n²) also shows that any such quadratic function is in O(n²).
What may be more surprising is that when a > 0, any linear function an + b is
in O(n²), which is easily veriﬁed by taking c = a + |b| and n₀ = max(1, −b/a).
title: O-notation
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
If you have seen O-notation before, you might ﬁnd it strange that we should
write, for example, n = O(n²). In the literature, we sometimes ﬁnd O-notation
informally describing asymptotically tight bounds, that is, what we have deﬁned
using Θ-notation. In this book, however, when we write f (n) = O(g(n)), we
are merely claiming that some constant multiple of g(n) is an asymptotic upper
bound on f (n), with no claim about how tight an upper bound it is. Distinguish-
ing asymptotic upper bounds from asymptotically tight bounds is standard in the
algorithms literature.
title: O-notation
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

merely by inspecting the algorithm’s overall structure. For example, the doubly
nested loop structure of the insertion sort algorithm from Chapter 2 immediately
yields an O(n²) upper bound on the worst-case running time: the cost of each it-
eration of the inner loop is bounded from above by O(1) (constant), the indices i

Since O-notation describes an upper bound, when we use it to bound the worst-
case running time of an algorithm, we have a bound on the running time of the algo-
rithm on every input—the blanket statement we discussed earlier. Thus, the O(n²)
bound on worst-case running time of insertion sort also applies to its running time
on every input. The Θ(n²) bound on the worst-case running time of insertion sort,
however, does not imply a Θ(n²) bound on the running time of insertion sort on
every input. For example, we saw in Chapter 2 that when the input is already
sorted, insertion sort runs in Θ(n) time.
title: O-notation

text:
Technically, it is an abuse to say that the running time of insertion sort is O(n²),
since for a given n, the actual running time varies, depending on the particular
input of size n. When we say “the running time is O(n²),” we mean that there is a
function f (n) that is O(n²) such that for any value of n, no matter what particular
input of size n is chosen, the running time on that input is bounded from above by
the value f (n). Equivalently, we mean that the worst-case running time is O(n²).
title: O-notation

Ω-notation
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a function, Ω-notation
provides an asymptotic lower bound.
title: Ω-notation
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
For a given function g(n), we denote
by Ω(g(n)) (pronounced “big-omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g
of n”) the set of functions
title: Ω-notation
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
Ω(g(n)) = {f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n₀ such that
0 ≤ cg(n) ≤ f (n) for all n ≥ n₀} .
Figure 3.1(c) shows the intuition behind Ω-notation. For all values n at or to the
right of n₀, the value of f (n) is on or above cg(n).
title: Ω-notation
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
From the deﬁnitions of the asymptotic notations we have seen thus far, it is easy
to prove the following important theorem (see Exercise 3.1-5).
title: Ω-notation
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
Theorem 3.1
For any two functions f (n) and g(n), we have f (n) = Θ(g(n)) if and only if
f (n) = O(g(n)) and f (n) = Ω(g(n)).
title: Theorem 3.1
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
As an example of the application of this theorem, our proof that an² + bn + c =
Θ(n²) for any constants a, b, and c, where a > 0, immediately implies that
an² + bn + c = Ω(n²) and an² +bn+c = O(n²). In practice, rather than using
Theorem 3.1 to obtain asymptotic upper and lower bounds from asymptotically
tight bounds, as we did for this example, we usually use it to prove asymptotically
tight bounds from asymptotic upper and lower bounds.
title: Theorem 3.1
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
When we say that the running time (no modiﬁer) of an algorithm is Ω(g(n)),
we mean that no matter what particular input of size n is chosen for each value
of n, the running time on that input is at least a constant times g(n), for sufﬁciently
large n. Equivalently, we are giving a lower bound on the best-case running time
of an algorithm. For example, the best-case running time of insertion sort is Ω(n),
which implies that the running time of insertion sort is Ω(n).
title: Theorem 3.1
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
The running time of insertion sort therefore belongs to both Ω(n) and O(n²),
since it falls anywhere between a linear function of n and a quadratic function of n.
Moreover, these bounds are asymptotically as tight as possible: for instance, the
running time of insertion sort is not Ω(n²), since there exists an input for which
insertion sort runs in Θ(n) time (e.g., when the input is already sorted). It is not
contradictory, however, to say that the worst-case running time of insertion sort

Asymptotic notation in equations and inequalities
We have already seen how asymptotic notation can be used within mathematical

might also write 2n² +3n+1 = 2n² +Θ(n). How do we interpret such formulas?

S1.1 Sorting as a precise contract

text:
Input, output, and identity
A sorting algorithm rearranges records according to a key and an ordering rule. For ascending
numeric order, every adjacent output pair must satisfy A[i] <= A[i+1]. The output must also
contain exactly the original records, including every repeated occurrence. These are independent
obligations: a sorted-looking array can still be wrong if it loses or duplicates a record.
The key is the part used for comparison; satellite data are the fields that travel with that key.
Sorting a list of (score, student_id) records by score must move each entire record. Sorting only
the score column destroys the association with the student. The ordering of equal scores is a
separate stability question.
title: Input, output, and identity
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.1 Sorting as a precise contract

text:
A contract before an implementation
State whether the function modifies the input, returns a fresh sequence, accepts an empty input,
and permits repeated keys. Define the comparator and its treatment of special values. A numeric
routine cannot silently switch to lexicographic string order: "10" precedes "2" lexicographically,
although 2 is smaller numerically.
For a comparator cmp, sortedness means cmp(A[i], A[i+1]) <= 0. Require a consistent ordering.
If the comparator gives contradictory results, no sorting algorithm can supply a meaningful
ordering guarantee.

title: S1.2 Stability, tie rules, and multiple keys
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.2 Stability, tie rules, and multiple keys

text:
What stability guarantees
A stable sort preserves the input order of records whose keys compare equal. Stability concerns
record identity, not whether repeated numeric values remain present. With input (2,a), (1,b),
(2,c), a stable ascending output places a before c. An unstable implementation may still be
completely correct under a contract requiring only sortedness and a permutation.
title: What stability guarantees
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.2 Stability, tie rules, and multiple keys

text:
Local rules with global consequences
Adjacent-swap bubble sort is stable when it swaps only if the left key is strictly greater.
Insertion sort is stable when it shifts only keys strictly greater than the saved key. A merge is
stable when it takes from the left run on equality. Stable counting sort using cumulative end
positions processes input from right to left. These rules are part of an implementation, not
consequences of the algorithm name alone.
The usual selection sort is unstable because a long-distance swap can move one record past an
equal record. Selecting the first minimum does not repair that effect. A stable selection variant
extracts the first minimum and shifts the intervening segment instead of exchanging the
endpoints.
title: Local rules with global consequences
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.2 Stability, tie rules, and multiple keys

text:
Multiple-key sorting
Suppose the required order is department first, then name. One option is a single lexicographic
comparator (department, name). Another is to sort stably by name and then stably by
department. The second pass preserves the established name order inside each department.
Reversing these passes changes the primary key.
If an explicit original-position field is appended to the comparison key, even an unstable
implementation can return the same tie order as a stable sort. That changes the comparator and
may require extra storage; it does not make the underlying implementation inherently stable.

text: S1.3 Cost models: time, space, and data movement
title: S1.3 Cost models: time, space, and data movement
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.3 Cost models: time, space, and data movement

text:
Choose the quantities being measured
Let n denote the number of records. Count key comparisons, swaps, shifts, writes, and auxiliary
storage separately. A swap of two array entries normally performs two array writes and uses one
temporary record; a shift performs one array write. Some conventions count the temporary
assignment as a third assignment. State the convention before comparing totals.
The RAM model assigns constant cost to basic operations on machine-sized values. Comparing
long strings, moving large records, or evaluating a costly key function can violate a simplistic
constant-cost assumption. Sorting indices or pointers may reduce movement of large payloads,
but the references still require storage and the output contract changes.
title: Choose the quantities being measured
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.3 Cost models: time, space, and data movement

text:
Auxiliary space versus input size
Bubble, ordinary selection, and array insertion sort use a constant number of temporary records,
giving O(1) auxiliary space under the standard model. A conventional array merge sort uses
O(n) temporary array storage and O(log n) recursion stack depth; its total auxiliary space is
O(n). Stable counting sort uses O(n+R) extra storage when R is the number of possible integer
keys.
Space complexity is peak simultaneously live storage. Allocating a new buffer at each recursive
call does not automatically imply O(n log n) peak memory; allocation lifetimes matter.
Repeated allocation can still increase total allocation traffic and practical overhead.
title: Auxiliary space versus input size
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.3 Cost models: time, space, and data movement

text:
Tradeoffs instead of one universal winner
Selection sort can reduce writes while still performing quadratic comparisons. Insertion sort can
exploit nearly sorted input. Merge sort gives a predictable worst-case bound but needs a buffer
in its standard array form. Counting sort depends on a suitably small integer range. A choice
must combine the input distribution, storage budget, tie-order requirement, and operation costs.

title: S1.4 Bounds, input cases, and average-case assumptions

S1.4 Bounds, input cases, and average-case assumptions

text:
Separate the function from its bound
Big-O is an asymptotic upper bound, Omega a lower bound, and Theta a tight bound. These
notations do not themselves mean worst, best, or average case. First define the cost function,
such as worst-case comparisons for inputs of length n, and then state a bound for that function.
The fixed-loop bubble sort from CLRS performs n(n-1)/2 key comparisons regardless of initial
order. Its best and worst running times are Theta(n^2), even though a sorted input needs no
swaps. Adding an early-exit flag changes the best running time to Theta(n), not its quadratic
worst case. An answer that simply says "bubble sort is linear in the best case" is incomplete
without naming the variant.
title: Separate the function from its bound
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.4 Bounds, input cases, and average-case assumptions
Separate the function from its bound

text:
Average is a model, not a typical-looking picture
For uniformly random permutations of n distinct keys, each pair is inverted with probability 1/2.
The expected number of inversions is therefore n(n-1)/4. Ordinary insertion sort has expected
quadratic time under this distribution, and adjacent-swap bubble sort has an expected quadratic
number of swaps.
Real inputs may have duplicates, long sorted runs, or a single displaced value. They need not
follow the uniform-permutation model. A claimed average bound should identify the
distribution, and a measured benchmark should identify the data generation process.

text: S1.5 Correctness: invariants, termination, and permutations
title: S1.5 Correctness: invariants, termination, and permutations
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.5 Correctness: invariants, termination, and permutations

text:
A complete proof has more than sortedness
To prove a sorting algorithm correct, establish that it terminates, preserves the input multiset or
record identities, and produces an ordered output. An array filled entirely with the smallest value
is sorted but usually violates preservation. A loop that would eventually establish sortedness is
not useful if its stopping rule can fail to terminate.
An invariant is a statement true at a designated point in each iteration. State that point precisely.
Prove initialization before the first iteration, maintenance from one iteration to the next, and the
useful consequence at termination. A decreasing nonnegative quantity or a finite loop range
supplies a separate termination argument.
title: A complete proof has more than sortedness
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.5 Correctness: invariants, termination, and permutations
A complete proof has more than sortedness

text:
Three different regions
Selection sort maintains a sorted prefix containing the smallest records. Insertion sort maintains
a sorted prefix containing exactly the records originally processed, which need not be globally
smallest. A right-to-left bubble pass establishes the next smallest record at the prefix boundary.
Confusing these statements leads to a proof that does not match the code.
For merging, the output prefix consists of the smallest consumed records from two already
sorted runs, and the next output record must be the smaller of the two unconsumed heads. For
counting sort, counts and cumulative positions reserve disjoint output intervals for each key.
title: Three different regions

Useful counterexamples
If an alleged invariant says the first insertion-sort prefix contains the global minimum, test input
[5,2,1] immediately after processing [5,2]. The prefix [2,5] is sorted but excludes 1. A small
counterexample often reveals an incorrect statement more clearly than an informal explanation.

S1.6 Input contracts and exceptional cases

text:
Empty, singleton, repeated, and signed keys
An empty sequence and a singleton are already sorted. Return them without invalid indexing.
Repeated keys must preserve multiplicities; all-equal input is useful for checking stability and
early termination. Comparison sorts naturally handle negative numbers when the comparator is
valid. Counting sort needs an explicit integer range and an offset for negative keys.
For a numeric comparator, special floating-point values require a deliberate policy. NaN does
not behave like an ordinary ordered number under usual numeric comparisons. Decide whether
such values are rejected, placed at an end, or handled by a defined total ordering. Do not assume
that an implementation designed for ordinary integers automatically establishes a valid
floating-point ordering.
title: Empty, singleton, repeated, and signed keys
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.6 Input contracts and exceptional cases
Empty, singleton, repeated, and signed keys

text:
Ascending, descending, and custom keys
For descending bubble sort, swap when the left key is smaller. For descending insertion sort,
shift keys smaller than the saved key. For descending selection sort, select a maximum. For
stable descending merge, choose the left run when keys are equal. Each adaptation changes the
strict direction while preserving the tie rule.
Counting sort can emit buckets in descending key order, but reversing the entire stable
ascending output reverses equal-key record order too. To preserve stability, reverse the order of
key groups while keeping each group's internal record order.

Specify zero-based or one-based indexing, whether ranges are inclusive or half-open, and
whether records are copied or rearranged in place. Avoid mixing these conventions inside one
procedure. If key extraction is expensive, caching keys is a separate memory-time tradeoff.

text:
From wording to a mathematical concept
The questions "keep equal items in their original order", "preserve ties", and "maintain arrival
order for repeated scores" ask about stability. "Use little extra memory", "sort in the same
array", and "avoid a buffer" concern auxiliary space. "Almost ordered", "few inversions", and
"small disorder" concern adaptivity, although they are not identical input descriptions.
Identify the concept and the implementation variant before retrieving a conclusion. A useful
answer records: algorithm, variant, input domain, indexing convention, comparator, cost
measure, bound, and stability rule. Missing conditions can convert a correct statement into a
misleading answer.
title: From wording to a mathematical concept

text:
Answer template
Begin with the direct result. State the condition that makes it true. Explain the mechanism using
the relevant invariant or loop. Supply a small example or counterexample. Distinguish the
guarantee from a measured performance claim. Point to a named section or figure for evidence
instead of guessing a universal ranking.
For "Why is bubble sort O(n) on sorted data?", first identify the early-exit variant. It performs
one pass with n-1 comparisons, observes no swaps, and stops. The fixed-loop CLRS variant
keeps all passes and is quadratic even on sorted data.
For "Does selection sort stop after finding the smallest item?", distinguish an individual scan
from the full algorithm. Each pass finds one minimum; the algorithm still repeats on the
remaining suffix. It ordinarily cannot know the minimum before inspecting every unexamined
suffix key.

S1.8 Choosing and validating a sorting method

text:
A decision based on the contract
Start with the data domain. Dense, bounded integer keys may justify counting sort, provided the
range array and output buffer fit memory. Arbitrary comparable records require a comparison
method. If a stable quadratic method is acceptable for small or nearly ordered input, insertion
sort is a useful candidate. Standard array merge sort supplies stable Theta(n log n) worst-case
time when a linear buffer is available.
Selection sort may be attractive in a constrained setting where writes are much more expensive
than comparisons and instability is acceptable. Bubble sort is particularly useful for teaching
local exchanges and invariants; its optimized variant recognizes sorted input, but it does not
provide a generally superior guarantee over insertion sort.
title: A decision based on the contract
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S1.8 Choosing and validating a sorting method
A decision based on the contract

text:
A compact comparison
Fixed-loop bubble: Theta(n^2) comparisons, O(1) space, stable under strict swaps. Early-exit
bubble: Theta(n) best time, Theta(n^2) worst time. Selection: Theta(n^2) comparisons in all
cases, at most n-1 nontrivial swaps, usually unstable. Insertion: Theta(n+I) time for I inversions,
stable under strict shifts. Standard merge: Theta(n log n) time, O(n) space, stable with left-first
ties. Counting: Theta(n+R) time, O(n+R) space in the stable output-array form.
title: A compact comparison

text:
Evidence from an implementation
Validate sortedness, identity preservation, and stability separately. Include empty, singleton,
all-equal, reversed, and nearly sorted inputs. Instrument comparisons and writes if the question
concerns costs. If timing is needed, use the same input copies and disclose input generation, key
types, and copy/allocation costs.

title: S2.1 Bubble sort: local exchanges and pass direction

S2.1 Bubble sort: local exchanges and pass direction

text:
The basic operation
Bubble sort repeatedly examines adjacent records and exchanges an out-of-order pair. For
ascending order, swap only when the left key is greater than the right key. Each exchange
removes exactly one inversion because the two records are adjacent and only their relative order
changes. A nonadjacent exchange does not have that same one-inversion property.
title: The basic operation
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.1 Bubble sort: local exchanges and pass direction

text:
The CLRS direction
Problem 2-2 scans from right to left in each inner loop. The smallest key in the remaining suffix
moves left through neighboring positions. After the pass for outer index i, A[i] contains a
smallest remaining key, and the finalized prefix grows by one.
Many presentations scan left to right instead. That version moves a largest remaining key
toward the right end and grows a finalized suffix. Both are bubble sort, but their intermediate
arrays and invariants differ. A trace question must specify the scan direction and what counts as
one pass.
title: The CLRS direction
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.1 Bubble sort: local exchanges and pass direction

text:
A right-to-left pass
For [5,1,4,2,8], start at the pair (2,8), which needs no swap. Then (4,2) swaps, giving [5,1,2,4,8].
The pair (1,2) needs no swap. Finally (5,1) swaps, giving [1,5,2,4,8]. The smallest key 1 is now
final at the left boundary. The suffix is not yet sorted.
The first pass need not leave the entire largest-to-smallest arrangement otherwise unchanged.
Several records may move, and some incidental positions may happen to be final. The invariant
guarantees one boundary record, not that exactly one record changes position.

The following procedure corresponds to the scan direction of CLRS, translated into zero-based

  n = length(A)

This alternative uses a shrinking right boundary and a flag that must be reset at the beginning of

No swaps during an entire pass mean all adjacent pairs in the active region are ordered. The
already finalized suffix is ordered and its keys are no smaller than those still active, so the
complete array is sorted. One comparison that needs no swap proves only that one pair is

text:
Follow the exact left-to-right early-exit procedure
Start with [5,1,4,2,8]. In pass 1, exchange (5,1), then (5,4), then (5,2), and leave (5,8)
unchanged. The array is [1,4,2,5,8]. Four comparisons and three swaps occurred. The right
boundary now excludes 8.
In pass 2, compare (1,4), exchange (4,2), and compare (4,5). The array becomes [1,2,4,5,8]. This
pass uses three comparisons and one swap. Because a swap occurred, the algorithm cannot stop
using the flag alone, even though the full array is now ordered.
In pass 3, compare (1,2) and (2,4). Neither pair swaps, so the algorithm stops. This pass uses
two comparisons and zero swaps. The complete execution uses nine key comparisons and four
swaps. A fixed-loop left-to-right version also performs the final one-comparison pass, giving ten
comparisons.

text:
Inner-loop invariant
Fix outer index i in the zero-based right-to-left version. Immediately before comparing A[j-1]
and A[j], A[j] is a smallest key among the records currently in positions j through n-1. Initially
j=n-1, so the statement holds for a singleton suffix.
After comparing and possibly exchanging the pair, A[j-1] is a smallest key of positions j-1
through n-1. If the left key is larger, the existing suffix minimum moves left; otherwise the left
key is itself no larger than every suffix key. Decrementing j establishes the invariant at the next
comparison.
When the inner loop ends, A[i] is a smallest key in the active suffix A[i..n-1]. Exchanges
preserve all records. Equal-key records may supply any minimum identity for this invariant; the
strict adjacent-swap rule gives stability separately.
title: Inner-loop invariant
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.4 Bubble sort: correctness of the CLRS version

text:
Outer-loop invariant
Before pass i, A[0..i-1] is sorted and contains the i smallest records by key, with every prefix
key no larger than every remaining suffix key. For i=0, the empty prefix makes the statement
trivially true. The inner pass puts a smallest remaining key at A[i], extending the prefix and
preserving the relation to the suffix.
After n-1 passes, the prefix contains the n-1 smallest records in order. The single remaining
record cannot be smaller than the prefix boundary, so the entire array is ordered. Both loops
have finite decreasing or increasing integer ranges, establishing termination. Each exchange is a
permutation, establishing preservation.

text: S2.5 Bubble sort: best, worst, and expected costs
title: S2.5 Bubble sort: best, worst, and expected costs
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.5 Bubble sort: best, worst, and expected costs

text:
Fixed comparisons
In the fixed-loop version the pass lengths are n-1, n-2, ..., 1. Their sum is n(n-1)/2. Consequently
key comparisons and running time are Theta(n^2) in both the best and worst cases under the
constant-cost RAM model. This statement remains true for already sorted and all-equal inputs,
despite zero swaps.
title: Fixed comparisons
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.5 Bubble sort: best, worst, and expected costs

text:
Exchanges and inversions
An inversion is a pair of positions p<q with key(A[p])>key(A[q]). Every strict adjacent
exchange removes exactly one inversion, and the sorted final array has none. Thus the total
number of exchanges is exactly the input inversion count I. With distinct reversed keys,
I=n(n-1)/2. With already ordered keys, I=0.
For a uniformly random permutation of distinct keys, each of the n(n-1)/2 pairs is inverted with
probability 1/2. Linearity of expectation gives E[I]=n(n-1)/4. An adjacent-swap implementation
therefore has expected quadratic exchange cost under this model.
title: Exchanges and inversions
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.5 Bubble sort: best, worst, and expected costs

text:
Early termination changes the best case
The early-exit version checks n-1 adjacent pairs and then stops on sorted input, giving Theta(n)
time for n>=2. Its worst case still uses quadratic comparisons and exchanges. Its average time
on uniformly random distinct permutations is also quadratic, since the expected swap count
alone is quadratic and the comparison count is bounded above by a quadratic sum.
One badly placed item can make a left-to-right version expensive even if the rest is ordered. In
[2,3,...,n,1], the smallest value moves left only one position per pass. There are n-1 inversions,
yet that direction still uses Theta(n^2) comparisons. Therefore a linear inversion count does not
imply linear bubble-sort time.

text: S2.6 Bubble sort: stability and record-safe exchanges
title: S2.6 Bubble sort: stability and record-safe exchanges
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.6 Bubble sort: stability and record-safe exchanges

text:
Why strict adjacent exchange is stable
Consider two equal-key records x and y, with x originally before y. Their relative order can
change only if they cross. In an adjacent-swap algorithm, crossing would require exchanging x
and y when they become neighbors. A condition that swaps only strictly out-of-order keys never
exchanges equal keys, so the order of x and y is preserved.
This proof depends on adjacency. Ordinary selection sort can reverse equal-key records by
exchanging a third record across them, even when it never directly swaps equal keys. A local
no-equality-swap condition alone does not establish stability for arbitrary exchanges.
title: Why strict adjacent exchange is stable
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.6 Bubble sort: stability and record-safe exchanges
Why strict adjacent exchange is stable

text:
An unstable modification
For input (2,a), (2,b), a left-to-right condition using >= rather than > exchanges the two records
even though their keys are already ordered. This violates stability. In an unbounded
repeat-until-no-swaps version, swapping equal keys can also prevent the no-swap termination
condition from ever occurring on an all-equal array.
title: An unstable modification
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.6 Bubble sort: stability and record-safe exchanges

text:
Move the whole record
If records contain key, id, and payload, exchanging only key fields produces corrupted
associations. A swap should rearrange entire records or references to records. If key evaluation
can change during sorting, the comparator contract is no longer fixed; materialize a consistent
key before sorting when appropriate.
For descending stable order, exchange adjacent records only when the left key is strictly smaller.
Equal-key record identities retain their original order. Reversing a stable ascending result is not
equivalent for records with repeated keys.

text: S2.7 Bubble sort: boundaries, variants, and common failures
title: S2.7 Bubble sort: boundaries, variants, and common failures
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.7 Bubble sort: boundaries, variants, and common failures

text:
Safe boundaries
In a zero-based left-to-right pass ending at end, iterate j from 0 through end-1, and compare A[j]
with A[j+1]. Using j=end reads beyond the active boundary. In the CLRS right-to-left version,
iterate j from n-1 down through i+1 and compare A[j-1] with A[j]. A loop that reaches j=0
would make j-1 invalid.
After a left-to-right pass, the maximum in the active region is final at end, so decrement end. Do
not shrink the left boundary in that same version without an additional proof. The opposite scan
direction finalizes a prefix instead.
title: Safe boundaries
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.7 Bubble sort: boundaries, variants, and common failures

text:
Useful adaptations
A last-swap boundary stores the right index of the last exchange during a left-to-right pass. All
pairs after that location were left ordered and the carried pass maximum makes the following
suffix final; the next active end can be that last exchange position. No exchanges mean
termination. This can reduce scanning without changing the quadratic worst case.
Cocktail or bidirectional bubble sort alternates left-to-right and right-to-left sweeps and
maintains boundaries at both ends. It helps transport small values toward the left as well as large
values toward the right. It remains a quadratic method in the worst case and is a different trace
from the single-direction listing.

text:
An in-place stable implementation
This function sorts a mutable list in place and returns it for convenience. A key function must be
consistent and produce mutually comparable values. The strict comparison implements stable
ascending order.

text:
Independent properties to check
Sortedness: every adjacent output key is nondecreasing. Preservation: each original record
identity occurs exactly once in the output. Stability: for every key, the sequence of identities in
the output equals the corresponding sequence in the input. Do not use a set comparison as a
multiplicity check; a set discards repeated occurrences.
For [5,1,4,2,8], the output is [1,2,4,5,8]. For labeled input [(2,'a'),(1,'b'),(2,'c')], using the first
tuple field as key yields [(1,'b'),(2,'a'),(2,'c')]. Empty and singleton lists return without a
comparison. The function does not validate NaN or a malformed comparator; those are contract
questions.

text: S2.9 Bubble sort: deep questions and counterexamples
title: S2.9 Bubble sort: deep questions and counterexamples
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.9 Bubble sort: deep questions and counterexamples

text:
How can a local algorithm establish global order?
Each completed pass places an extremal remaining record at a final boundary. The outer
invariant grows that final region until no unresolved region remains. Alternatively, a complete
no-swap pass directly establishes that every active adjacent pair is ordered. Transitivity of the
ordering then establishes global order within the region.
title: How can a local algorithm establish global order?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.9 Bubble sort: deep questions and counterexamples
How can a local algorithm establish global order?

text:
Why is it inferior to insertion sort on a displaced minimum?
For left-to-right early-exit bubble sort, [2,3,...,n,1] requires the minimum to travel left one step
per pass, yielding quadratic comparisons. Insertion sort saves 1 once and shifts the preceding
n-1 records in one insertion, giving linear work for this input. Both perform work related to n-1
inversions, but their scans impose different overhead.
title: Why is it inferior to insertion sort on a displaced minimum?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.9 Bubble sort: deep questions and counterexamples
Why is it inferior to insertion sort on a displaced minimum?

text:
Can the number of passes identify the algorithm?
Not by itself. Selection and bubble can each finalize one boundary record per pass. Inspect the
mechanism: bubble exchanges adjacent inverted pairs throughout a scan; selection scans for an
extremum and usually performs one long-distance swap. The pass direction and early-exit rule
further determine trace behavior.
title: Can the number of passes identify the algorithm?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.9 Bubble sort: deep questions and counterexamples
Can the number of passes identify the algorithm?

text:
Does swapping remove exactly one inversion every time?
Only a strict adjacent exchange has that guarantee. If equal adjacent records are exchanged, no
strict inversion is removed. A distant selection-sort exchange may change many pair orders at
once. The exact inversion argument must name both the comparison and adjacency conditions.
title: Does swapping remove exactly one inversion every time?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S2.9 Bubble sort: deep questions and counterexamples
Does swapping remove exactly one inversion every time?

text:
Can bubble sort be useful beyond teaching?
It can be implemented with constant auxiliary storage and a simple local swap rule. A
constrained use should justify why those properties matter and why the quadratic worst case is
acceptable. Its simplicity is not evidence that it is the fastest general-purpose sorter.
title: Can bubble sort be useful beyond teaching?

"Will it stop immediately when sorted?" The early-exit listing needs a full no-swap certification
pass; fixed-loop CLRS does not stop early. "Does it work on duplicates?" Yes, preserve
occurrences and swap strictly for stability. "What if only one element is misplaced?" Its travel
direction and displacement matter; that phrase alone does not guarantee few comparisons.

title: S3.1 Selection sort: finding the next extremum

S3.1 Selection sort: finding the next extremum

text:
Selection rather than adjacent exchange
Selection sort divides the array into a finalized sorted prefix and an unresolved suffix. On pass i,
inspect every record in the suffix and remember the position of a smallest key. Exchange that
record with A[i]. Continue until only one unresolved record remains.
The scan determines where the minimum is; it does not need to rearrange the array while
searching. This is the essential distinction from bubble sort, which performs local exchanges
during its scan. Both can move a minimum to the left boundary, but selection uses one direct
exchange rather than a chain of adjacent exchanges.
title: Selection rather than adjacent exchange

  for i = 0 to length(A)-2
    m = i
    for j = i+1 to length(A)-1

        m = j

Remembering only the minimum key is insufficient when a complete record must be moved.
The index m identifies the record and its satellite fields. Reset m=i at each pass; otherwise a

Strict < chooses the first encountered minimum among equal candidates. Nevertheless, the
distant exchange can disrupt the order of equal records elsewhere. Tie selection and algorithmic

text: S3.3 Selection sort: proof of correctness
title: S3.3 Selection sort: proof of correctness
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S3.3 Selection sort: proof of correctness

text:
Inner search invariant
Immediately before processing candidate index j, m identifies a smallest-key record among
positions i through j-1. Initially m=i and the scanned interval contains one record. Comparing
A[j] with A[m] and updating m only for a smaller key extends the minimum property to
positions i through j.
At the end of the scan, m identifies a minimum in the whole active suffix. The scan only reads
records and changes an index, so it preserves their positions and identities.
title: Inner search invariant
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S3.3 Selection sort: proof of correctness

text:
Outer invariant
Before pass i, the prefix A[0..i-1] is ordered, contains i smallest-key records, and every prefix
key is no greater than every suffix key. The prefix is empty for i=0, so initialization holds.
Exchanging A[i] with the suffix minimum places a smallest remaining key after the existing
prefix. The enlarged prefix remains ordered and no larger than the new suffix.
The displaced A[i] remains in the suffix; an exchange cannot lose it. A self-swap can be skipped
without changing the proof. After n-1 passes, one record remains. The outer invariant forces that
record to be no smaller than every key in the prefix, establishing sortedness. Every swap
preserves the collection of records, and finite loop bounds establish termination.
title: Outer invariant
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S3.3 Selection sort: proof of correctness

text:
Why the globally-smallest clause matters
An ordered prefix alone is insufficient. For example, [4,5 | 1,2] has a sorted prefix but it cannot
be considered final. In selection sort, the invariant rules this state out because the prefix keys
exceed suffix keys. Insertion sort is allowed to have that kind of relationship while it is still
processing later records.
title: Why the globally-smallest clause matters

text:
At most one nontrivial swap per pass
With the m!=i guard, there are at most n-1 nontrivial swaps and at most 2(n-1) array-slot writes
from those swaps. This is an upper bound, not an exact count for every input. An already sorted
array needs zero such swaps. A version that self-swaps makes exactly n-1 swap calls, which is a
different counting convention.
Few swaps do not imply a small number of comparisons. A reverse array of eight distinct keys
still needs 28 comparisons even though the minimum exchange mechanism can fix more than
one position per swap. Never substitute the bubble-sort inversion swap formula for selection's
distant exchanges.

text:
When writes are expensive
A cost expression can be written as C_cmp * n(n-1)/2 + C_swap * s + lower-order overhead,
where 0<=s<=n-1. If moving a record is expensive relative to comparing its key, the linear swap
bound can matter. Sorting pointers may further reduce payload movement, although that
approach changes representation and may require extra storage.
Selection is not automatically the best write-minimizing algorithm among all possibilities. The
bound here compares a particular standard method with the other elementary methods in this
supplement; it is not a universal lower bound on writes.

text:
A minimal counterexample
Use records (2,a), (2,b), (1,c), sorted by the numeric field. The first pass chooses (1,c) as the
minimum and exchanges it with (2,a). The array becomes (1,c), (2,b), (2,a). The next pass sees
two equal keys and makes no strict-smaller update. The final output places b before a, reversing
their original order.
The output remains numerically sorted and preserves all identities. It is the stability requirement,
and only that additional requirement, that fails. Using plain [2,2,1] hides the failure because the
two equal numbers cannot be distinguished.
title: A minimal counterexample
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S3.5 Selection sort: why the usual exchange is unstable

text:
Why first-minimum selection is not enough
The inner loop with strict < already selects the first occurrence of a minimum. The instability
above happens because a nonminimum record is displaced across an equal-key record by the
long-distance swap. Changing only how equal minima are chosen cannot eliminate all such
crossings.
Choosing the last minimum with <= can create other instability. For an all-equal array, it may
exchange a boundary record with a later equal record. Both the selection rule and the movement
operation have to be examined.
title: Why first-minimum selection is not enough

text:
Change the movement, not just the tie test
Find the first minimum in the active suffix using strict <. Save that complete record. Shift
positions i through m-1 one place to the right, preserving their relative order, then put the saved
minimum at i. This removes the endpoint swap that caused instability.
title: Change the movement, not just the tie test
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

STABLE-SELECTION(A)
  for i = 0 to length(A)-2
    m = i
    for j = i+1 to length(A)-1
      if key(A[j]) < key(A[m])
        m = j
    if m != i
      saved = A[m]

text:
Why equal records retain order
The first minimum precedes every other equal minimum still active. Placing it at the boundary
does not cross an earlier equal minimum. The shift moves every intervening record together and
does not reverse their mutual order. Repeating this reasoning establishes stable extraction for
every key group.
For (2,a), (2,b), (1,c), save c and shift a and b right. The result is (1,c), (2,a), (2,b), unlike the
ordinary-swap result. The globally-smallest-prefix proof for selection still applies, with
permutation preservation supplied by extraction plus shifting.
title: Why equal records retain order
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements

text:
The tradeoff
Auxiliary storage remains O(1) records. The minimum searches still perform n(n-1)/2
comparisons. However, shifting can require Theta(n^2) array writes in the worst case. Thus the
ordinary selection sort's linear bound on nontrivial swaps does not translate into a linear
movement bound for this stable variant.

text:
Common failures
Reset m for each outer pass. Search only the unresolved suffix, including its final position. Do
not place a swap inside every candidate comparison and still describe the result as the one-swap
selection algorithm; that mutation is a different procedure with a different movement count.
The array can be empty: range(-1) produces no iterations in this Python listing. A singleton
similarly needs no pass. For descending order, update m when the candidate key is strictly
larger. For record sorting, exchange whole records and do not rewrite only their keys.

text:
Why must the suffix be scanned even if the prefix is ordered?
An ordered prefix is already finalized by the invariant, but the next smallest key can be
anywhere in the suffix. Without extra information about key values or their arrangement, every
candidate can affect which record must be selected. The fixed scan therefore performs the same
number of comparisons on ordered and disordered input.
title: Why must the suffix be scanned even if the prefix is ordered?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S3.8 Selection sort: deep questions and neighboring concepts
Why must the suffix be scanned even if the prefix is ordered?

text:
Why do n-1 passes suffice?
After n-1 passes, the prefix contains the n-1 smallest records in order, every remaining key is no
smaller than the prefix, and exactly one record remains. That record necessarily occupies the
final position. A last minimum search on a singleton provides no new information.
title: Why do n-1 passes suffice?
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S3.8 Selection sort: deep questions and neighboring concepts

text:
Selection sort versus selecting one rank
The name selection sort does not mean an optimal selection algorithm for the kth smallest
element. Sorting the entire array is more work than needed if only one rank is requested. After k
passes, ordinary selection has finalized the k smallest records, but this partial method costs
O(kn) comparisons and is not a general linear-time rank-selection guarantee.
title: Selection sort versus selecting one rank
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S3.8 Selection sort: deep questions and neighboring concepts
Selection sort versus selecting one rank

text:
Selection versus insertion
Selection finds an extremum in the unresolved suffix and finalizes a boundary record. Insertion
takes the next record from the original processing order and inserts it into a sorted processed
prefix. A selection prefix is globally smallest; an insertion prefix need not be. Both can use
constant auxiliary storage, yet their adaptivity and stability rules differ.
title: Selection versus insertion
heading_path: Basic Sorting Algorithms — English source and labeled supplements
S3.8 Selection sort: deep questions and neighboring concepts

text:
Selection versus bubble
One long-distance selection swap may remove many inversions and may cross equal-key
identities. Each strict adjacent bubble swap removes exactly one inversion and preserves
equal-key order. An answer based only on "both move the minimum" overlooks these
consequences.
